newsitem.title: USA: Amtrak trains up and running after derailment.
newsitem.headline: Amtrak trains up and running after derailment.

text.p: Amtrak reopened full train service along its busy northeast corridor Sunday after the link between Newark and New York City's Penn Station was cleared from a derailed passenger train, officials said.

Six cars of a 14-car passenger train travelling from Washington to Boston plunged down an embankment early Saturday into a marsh near the Hackensack River drawbridge, about three miles west of New York City, disrupting traffic for more than 24 hours.
The accident caused no serious injuries, but 32 people were treated and released at area hospitals.

Amtrak spokeswoman Isabel Kaldenbach, Amtrak's director of communications for the northeast corridor, said one of the two tracks was cleared at 9:35 a.m. EST Sunday, and the second track was expected to be cleared in time for Monday morning's commuting hour, she said.
Trains were experiencing minor delays of five to seven minutes, she said.
The derailment Saturday involved two locomotives, one mail car and three passenger cars.

A second passenger train, The Carolinian, heading south to Charlotte, N.C., from New York City was sideswiped by the careening cars of the derailed train as it went by on the adjacent track but no one was injured on that train, the spokeswoman said.
The southbound train went on to Newark, N.J., where passengers changed trains. Service between Newark and New York on Amtrak's busiest line was disrupted for most of Saturday.

Two Amtrak employees, admitted to area hospitals for observation after the accident, were expected to be released Sunday, the spokeswoman said. She said area hospitals had given Amtrak an incorrect figure of 35 passengers treated in their original report.

Sen. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, who was briefed by safety officials told reporters at the scene Saturday, said the derailment may have been caused by an improper alignment of the track. "The track did not connect as it should," he said.
National Transportation Safety Board investigators will look into the operation of the drawbridge as a possible cause of the derailment, NTSB spokesman Peter Goelz told Reuters.

"We are going to be looking into the operation of the drawbridge. We understand that there were some difficulties with the drawbridge (early Saturday morning) and that certainly is going to be one of the important areas," he said.

The New York Times in its Sunday edition said that investigators quoted an unnamed bridge operator as saying he had been unable to fully open the bridge for a tugboat with a barge that passed through 2 1/2 hours before the derailment. The Times said the operator believed he had fully closed the tight-fitting rails on the bridge.
